reason: The sources provide multiple confirming details regarding its discovery, physical properties, and the process of its destruction by stellar radiation.
story: In 1888, Williamina Fleming, a former maid working as a 'computer' at Harvard, discovered a strange silhouette on a photographic plate. This 3-light-year-tall pillar of cold dust and gas, now known as the Horsehead Nebula or Barnard 33, sits roughly 1,400 light-years away in the constellation Orion. It isn't a solid object but a dense cloud blocking the light of the glowing red hydrogen gas behind it, known as IC 434. Though it appears eternal, the Horsehead is a temporary ghost. Powerful ultraviolet radiation from the nearby star system Sigma Orionis is relentlessly carving into the dust. This 'photo-evaporation' process is sculpting the cloud into its iconic shape, but it is also destroying it. Astronomers estimate the pillar is being eroded so quickly that it will completely disintegrate within a few million years, leaving only a scattered nursery of newly born stars behind.
angle: The iconic Horsehead Nebula is actually a 3-light-year-tall tower of dust currently being evaporated by the radiation of nearby stars, and it will eventually vanish entirely.

claims.claim: The Horsehead Nebula was discovered by Williamina Fleming in 1888.
It was identified on a photographic plate at the Harvard College Observatory.
The nebula is cataloged as Barnard 33.
It is located in the constellation of Orion.
The Horsehead is situated just south of the star Alnitak (Zeta Orionis) in Orion's Belt.
The nebula is a dark cloud of dust and gas that blocks light from stars behind it.
It is visible because it is silhouetted against the bright emission nebula IC 434.
The red background glow is caused by ionized hydrogen gas.
The nebula is approximately 1,300 to 1,600 light-years away from Earth.
The pillar is roughly 3 light-years in dimension.
The nebula is being eroded by ultraviolet radiation from nearby stars.
The star Sigma Orionis is the primary source of radiation ionizing the nearby gas.
The structure is an active site of star formation.
The Horsehead is considered one of the most difficult objects to see visually with an amateur telescope.

disputed: The exact distance to the nebula varies by source, with values ranging from 1,300 light-years (S3, S5) to 1,600 light-years (S2, S6); the script should use an approximate value like 'roughly 1,400 light-years.'

The remaining lifespan of the nebula is disputed; S3 estimates 5 million years, while S4 states structures like it are destroyed on timescales of typically a few thousand years. The script should attribute the 5 million year figure to specific recent estimates.
The exact height is reported as 2.2 light-years (S2) and 4 light-years (S5); the script should use 'roughly 3 light-years' as a middle ground.
